title: You Can't Model What You Can't Locate: A Building-Level View of U.S. Data Center Risk
summary: Data centers are among the fastest-growing concentrations of insured value, but the industry has limited exposure data to underwrite data center insurance.
body_markdown:
*The industry is writing one of the fastest-growing concentrations of insured value with some of its thinnest location level data.*


The (re)insurance industry is adding huge amounts of insured value from data centers to their portfolios faster than almost any other occupancy and tracking it with significantly less location level information than most basic commercial and industrial occupancies. Northern Virginia alone holds hundreds of these facilities, many on campuses where a single street address by a cedent often represents multiple individual data center structures. View that campus and those facilities at the building level and the picture changes: billions of dollars in insured value, stacked into pockets a single hailstorm could cross in an afternoon, and accumulation, geocoding, and occupancy questions that single address-level data could never answer. This isn’t just a regional story. Data centers are in development all over the U.S., with many written without proper geocoding or physical and operational attributes.


The stakes are rising with this buildout. The global data center insurance market is forecast to more than double, from around $11 billion today to over $24 billion by 2030, according to[Allianz Commercial.](https://reinsurancene.ws/data-centre-insurance-market-forecast-to-exceed-24bn-by-2030-allianz) Yet most insurers and reinsurers still assess these facilities with incomplete or no location data.


## What do insurers need to know about data center risk?


As we've engaged with the industry on data center risk, three needs continually surface.


**Which building(s)?** Hyperscale and large colocation facilities typically sit on campuses, where a single address can cover multiple buildings across a wide area. Traditional address-level geocoding can return a single point for the entire campus, often a parcel centroid or street segment, so multiple buildings collapse into a single coordinate, and accumulation analysis quietly inherits the error: a hazard footprint that clips some of those buildings reads as hitting all of them or none. The industry lacks building level geocoding to be able to accurately assess insured limits and aggregates effectively, particularly in high concentration areas that have many data center campuses in close proximity.


**What type of data center is being underwritten?** Physical and operational attributes drive commercial underwriting decisions, and data center type can fundamentally change this process. A colocation facility for example, owned by a single operator, leased to multiple named insureds, each with expensive electronic equipment and its own unique time-element exposure, can lead to a stacking of limits at a single data center far in excess of a (re)insurer’s underwriting and capacity appetites. Without individual building level information, assessing this risk can be challenging.


**Where is their accumulation?** Insurers want to understand how much exposed value is held in one data center location across multiple diverse portfolios including primary property, inland marine, excess property, casualty and reinsurance books. And the question extends beyond building and contents. Time-element exposures, including sub limits such as expediting expense, ordinance or law, and utility interruption, can magnify a portfolio's true concentration well beyond what the property schedule suggests.


## What does building-level data center exposure data look like?


Managing this risk starts with actual buildings, their footprints, latitude/longitude and then building level physical and operational attributes such as construction, capacity, redundancy etc. If you can't locate the buildings appropriately then managing the view of risk to perils becomes quite challenging. In addition, as we have engaged with many of our clients, there is concern that data centers are already included in their portfolios potentially under general commercial or industrial (non-data center specific) occupancy types.


That conviction shaped the Verisk U.S. Data Center Exposure Database: building-level detail on more than 2,500 individual U.S. data center facilities, with priority on hyperscale and colocation sites. Among the many questions this data set can help answer, here are three:


**Precise building location** : each of these structures carries a Verisk GeoPin geocode placed at the rooftop centroid and a footprint shapefile that can be used in geospatial tools to view and match existing portfolio exposure data. A five-building campus, for example, will include five distinct data center buildings and attributes as well as shapefiles and geocodes so you will be able to view the campus in more detail than the single address point.


**What are they actually underwriting:** physical attributes are captured at the building rather than the campus level: area, construction type, year built, and stories, plus the operational attributes that matter most to underwriting and aggregation: capacity, power and cooling redundancy, operator, and facility type. In addition, this data set includes both operational data centers and under-construction pre-operational data centers to ensure a full view of aggregation across business units.


**Where is their accumulation:** with footprints and attributes for these U.S. data center facilities the (re)insurers can match this database against their own various books of business to find areas of concentration and areas of potential growth. In addition, this data set allows for the ability to better analyze non-data center occupancy types and distinguish between locations that are in close proximity to a data center and those that are not.


Because the market itself is a moving target, the database is updated every six months, with status indicators that track facilities from construction through operation, so a building breaking ground today is already on the map when the submission arrives.


## Which hazards pose the greatest risk to data centers in the U.S.?


Based on the geographic spread of operational and planned data center construction in the U.S., this occupancy class is exposed to all natural catastrophe perils. As a result, we plan to supplement our data set with hazard information at the building level to allow for more detailed aggregation and exposure management analysis at the building and peril levels.
